body.text: In China’s electric vehicle industry, suppliers have been silently suffering. An investigation by Economic Observer carried out in September of this year examined financial data from 14 automakers, finding that their average accounts-payable and notes-payable turnover period had risen from 164.4 days at the end of 2025 to 187.5 days in the first half of 2026. This means that automakers have been taking longer to pay their suppliers, who need the funds to pay workers and purchase production inputs. This may cause many suppliers to borrow money to cover their everyday costs.

After 17 major vehicle manufacturers promised to limit supplier payment periods to 60 days last year, Beijing introduced new rules in September 2026 to govern how automakers pay their suppliers. This may be working; according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, the average payment period was 54, about 10 days shorter than a year earlier.

This does seemingly contradict the findings of the Economic Observer, but it should be pointed out that they use two different measures. The industry association measured time from acceptance of an invoice until payment, including payment by certain bank bills, while the financial statement measure used by the journal uses accounts payable, including acceptance bills, and cost of goods sold. It may overstate payment periods because it includes acceptance bills while excluding the cost of unsold products. However, it does point to the fact that suppliers may receive a financial instrument instead of cash, while delays in inspection or invoice processing can further extend the wait.

The supplier payment issue is not limited to the automotive sector. As Cao Yuanyuan, director general of the People’s Bank of China’s Financial Market Department, acknowledged in a September 14 government briefing, large companies with substantial cash reserve have delayed supplier payments, forcing smaller suppliers to borrow to continue operating. This represents a transfer of financing costs from larger to smaller firms.

This highlights an inequality that often goes under the radar in China’s manufacturing sector. Large firms can reduce their need for working capital by becoming more efficient, but also by taking longer to pay their suppliers, moving the financial burden up the supply chain. In some cases, large companies have issued a digital promise to pay later, which the supplier presents to a bank to obtain a loan. This practice has sometimes been abused by companies looking to postpone cash payments while charging suppliers financing fees.

These outstanding certificates reached 3 trillion yuan at their peak, but had fallen to 2.4 trillion yuan by July 2026, according to the central bank. Average payment periods for the certificates had fallen to 92 days, which demonstrates progress but considerable scale of such arrangements.

For context, at the end of September 2026, large industrial firms held 29.77 trillion yuan in accounts receivable, a year-on-year increase of 10 percent. Their average collection period was about 72 days. This illustrates how much working capital is tied up in unpaid invoices in China’s manufacturing industry.

Why does this matter? True, longer payment periods require suppliers to borrow and pay financing costs, but suppliers also may have to postpone growth and innovation. Suppliers may also be forced to accept less favorable contract terms to keep large customers. This is detrimental to industries that rely on smaller manufacturers in particular, since postponing supplier payments reduces the capabilities of the supplier pool.

However, it seems that Chinese officials recognize these risks. According to the September automotive regulations, most production materials must be inspected within three working days and automakers may not force suppliers to accept certain noncash payment instruments. They also encourage firms to pay smaller suppliers within 30 to 60 days. A State Council directive called for even broader reforms, including tighter oversight of electronic certificates and greater scrutiny of large companies with substantial payables.

Despite this, enforcement of these measures remains challenging, as firms in highly competitive industries may attempt other ways to lower their costs, such as negotiating lower prices from their suppliers. These actions would also constrain suppliers’ financial health and innovation.

For international businesses looking to source from China, these cash flow issues may reduce supplier flexibility, which can prevent the overseas firm from responding to growing demand. A supplier may have the capabilities required by a large multinational, but a lack of cash may prohibit them from investing in improvements or expanding capacity to meet international market demand. Buying firms therefore need to assess the financial health of their suppliers, not just their existing capacity and delivery performance.

China’s competitive place in global manufacturing disguises a tension beneath the surface: large manufacturers may gain market share but potentially at the expense of the very suppliers that keep them in business. Whether Beijing can ensure supplier protection while preserving the competitiveness of large manufacturers will test the policymaking skills of China’s technocrats.
